catalog_quote: Tina Sambal has 14 consonants and 3 vowels: a, b, k, d, g, h, i, l, m, n, ng, o, p, r, s, t, w. There is also a glottal stop which is written in this dictionary with a hyphen word-medially (e.g. mag-atap "be careful", ba-yo "new") and with accent marks word-finally (e.g. stressed: konâ "fish", unstressed: lolò "sadness"). Stress is important in each Tina Sambal word, as shown in the following examples: final stress without glottal stop halá "dare you!" penultimate stress without glottal stop hala "horn" final stress with glottal stop lakô "many" penultimate stress with glottal stop lakò "merchandise"

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Tina Sambal has an empty rule; this supplies the placement: contrastive penult vs final stress with minimal pairs. No existing statement to agree or disagree with.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically contrastive between the final and the penultimate syllable (minimal pairs halá 'dare you!' vs hala 'horn'; lakô 'many' vs lakò 'merchandise'), independently of the presence of a final glottal stop; the Philippine penult/ultima type. Orthographic convention: acute = stressed final open syllable, circumflex = stressed final syllable with glottal stop, grave = unstressed final syllable with glottal stop, unmarked = penultimate stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All statements concern Tina Sambal proper (northern Zambales towns Iba, Palauig, Masinloc, Candelaria, Sta. Cruz, plus Infanta in Pangasinan). The dictionary's native compiler is from Masinloc; Goschnick's data come from Candelaria, Masinloc and Sta. Cruz. Goschnick notes a segmental dialect split (Sta. Cruz/Infanta has s where the other towns have h) but no dialect difference in stress.

new_statements.quote: p. 40: "(Words with closed syllables in penultimate positions are neutral in regard to stress except for contracted forms.)" p. 43: "in longer words where every other syllable received stress, it seemed sufficient if one of the syllables with a secondary stress earlier in the word had been made prominent by the melody" p. 47: "Tina Sambal native speakers react against misplaced stress only when it occurs in words where changing the stress would result in a different meaning." p. 403: "Word-final glottal stops are combined with the notation of stress: acute [´] for stressed final open syllables, grave [`] for unstressed final syllables ending in a glottal stop, circumflex [^] for stressed final syllables ending in a glottal stop. These accent marks are not used in ordinary writing."

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the 1988 dictionary's contrastive penult/final placement and adds detail: closed-penult neutrality, alternating secondary stress, stress-conditioned aspiration of final open syllables; fills the catalog's empty rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexical (final vs penultimate) and can distinguish meanings; native speakers object to misplaced stress only where it changes meaning. Words whose penult is a closed syllable are 'neutral' with respect to stress (no penult/ultima contrast there) except in contracted forms. Longer words carry alternating secondary stresses (every other syllable). Also p. 37: final open syllables often become aspirated when stressed. Marking convention as in the 1988 dictionary.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'in longer words where every other syllable received stress.. one of the syllables with a secondary stress earlier in the word' (p. 43), i.e. alternating secondary stress preceding the main stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Closed-penult words are neutral in regard to stress (p. 40); contracted forms excepted; musical stress in songs overrides word stress (pp. 40-47, poetic performance only).
